links.note: Procopius, a hostile witness to Justinian, says the emperor ordered heresies such as the Montanists' to be given up. He reports that the Montanists of Phrygia shut themselves in their churches and burned them. A law of Justinian also names the Montanists.

links.note: John Chrysostom was made bishop of Constantinople. Socrates says it was the emperor's court that chose him. The chamberlain Eutropius told Theophilus of Alexandria to consecrate John or face trial. Back in 381 the emperor had made a law. It named the bishops whose communion marked a Catholic church, and Diodore of Tarsus was one of them.

links.outcome: After synods condemned John Chrysostom, his followers left the church. They met on their own and were known as the Johannites.
links.note: Two synods condemned John Chrysostom. Then the emperor barred him from his own church. Two months later, as Socrates writes, 'a decree of the emperor sent him into exile'.

links.outcome: The Second Council of Constantinople cursed Theodore of Mopsuestia. It also cursed all who stood up for him or said the way he read Scripture was orthodox.
links.note: In 553 a council at Constantinople condemned Theodore of Mopsuestia by name. He had been dead for more than a hundred years. Its twelfth canon curses anyone who defends him or says his reading of Scripture is orthodox.

links.note: The Augsburg Confession of 1530 calls on Chrysostom as a witness to how the early church shared Communion. Melanchthon wrote a defense of the Confession, known as the Apology. In it he quotes a saying of Chrysostom. It runs: contrition in the heart, confession in the mouth, humility in the work.

links.note: Jerome and Rufinus had once been close friends. Around 400 they broke for good over Rufinus's Latin translation of Origen. Each wrote a defense against the other. Rufinus said their friendship had been mended only with difficulty. Jerome complained that an old friend he had made peace with now attacked him.

sources.work: Rufinus, Apology to Apronianus (against Jerome), Book II, section 42 (written at Aquileia, 400, per the translators' heading)

links.outcome: At Aquileia the bishops condemned Palladius. They found him unworthy to be a priest, and said a Catholic must be made bishop in his place.
links.note: The Council of Aquileia met in 381. There the city's own bishop, Valerian, spoke out against Palladius, who was a Homoian bishop. He said that whoever defends Arius is an Arian. And whoever will not condemn the blasphemies of Arius, he added, is a blasphemer as well. The council condemned both Palladius and Secundianus.

links.note: At Aquileia in 381, Ambrose led the questioning of Palladius, a Homoian bishop. Palladius would not condemn a letter of Arius, so Ambrose had it read out. In Milan in 386 he preached against Auxentius, a rival bishop who was also Homoian. He declared him cast out.

Gregory saw it as Hilary's help against 'those heretics' he had once fought. He calls Hilary a defender of the Trinity who was sent into exile for its sake.

links.outcome: Justinian banned Donatists, Arians, Jews and pagans from having places to meet. Nor could they hold rites as the church does.
links.note: In 535 the emperor Justinian made a law for Africa, which his armies had won back. It named the Donatists along with Arians, Jews and pagans, and barred them from holding services. In the 590s Pope Gregory the Great wrote to the emperor Maurice. He praised the orders Maurice had given against the Donatists.

links.note: Theodoret, who wrote in the fifth century, says Bishop Leontius of Antioch made Aetius a deacon. Two ascetics of the city, Flavian and Diodore, protested in public that this brought shame on the church. Leontius then suspended Aetius.

links.note: Kievan Rus' took its Christian books and its letters from the Cyril and Methodius mission. Mouravieff, a Russian church historian writing in 1838, says the brothers' Slavonic Bible later helped win the Russians to the faith. Herberstein retold the Rus' annals in 1549. He says the Rus' began to write down their past once the Slavonic letters came.

links.note: In December 1367 at Erfurt, a beghard called John Hartmann was questioned by Walter Kerling, named by the pope's authority to try heresy. links.outcome: Rome recognized Mutran Hanna as head of the Chaldeans on one condition: he must make none of his kin bishops. That ended passing the office down in one family.
links.note: George Percy Badger, a clergyman who lived at Mosul, wrote in 1852 that the Pope recognized Mutran Hanna as head of all the Chaldeans.
